units.title: Supply boat out to the Holm this morning.
units.author: sb_commuter_lisle
units.text: From the 07:10: the contractor's workboat left Gilliver at about 06:35, well loaded, and was lying off the Holm landing by the time we passed Lisle point. Somebody on the ferry rail said they were bringing bunks back already. I could not see any bunks from a ferry. I'm posting this because the thread asked for observations, not because I find boats interesting.

units.author: skeptic_ferrous
units.text: Thank you; that is the right kind of post. A contractor sending back plant it no longer needs before the final day is ordinary demobilisation. So is sending extra fuel out for a last push. Both are consistent with finished, nearly finished and not finished. That is the trouble with watching boats: they always look busy.

units.author: truthwatch_gil
units.text: Bunks out means they're not coming back to that camp. Or bunks in means more people going out. Either way someone on that ferry saw bunks. I've sent it round my list. Whatever the company does on the 31st, remember you read it here first, before the Courier.

units.author: retired_teacher
units.text: Nobody saw bunks. The original post says that somebody said they saw bunks, which is a different sentence entirely, and a distinction I spent thirty-four years teaching ten-year-olds. Most of them had it by Easter.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: Thank you for the distinction. I would add that the original post is exactly the kind I asked for, with the hearsay clearly marked as hearsay. Second-hand bunks are not a source. Please keep it that way, all of you.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Bunks. Lads. It's a work boat with stuff on it going to a work site and coming back. That is the whole story. Grow up, the lot of you.

units.author: gilliver_lamp
units.text: The boat went out before it was light and came back about half past nine. I was at the window with my tea. There were things on deck under a green sheet. I couldnt say what. The skipper waved to someone on the wall the way they do, so I waved too, though I dont suppose he saw.

units.author: trades_holm_work
units.text: Demob usually goes like this: chipper and spare saws back first, fuel and the main saws last. If they sent fuel out today theyre still cutting. If they brought the chipper back theyre close to done. Could be both. I would do both, if I was them and the boat was paid for.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Green sheet was over spare saws and some yard gear, near enough. I was alongside at the fuel berth. Diesel went out as well. So they're still at it, and they're tidying up. Both. That's all I know, and more than I ought to say about other folk's work.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: For the boat-watchers: visibility today was over 30 km, wind under 5 knots, sea smooth, pressure 1035 hPa. If anyone wanted to move a lot of kit to or from the Holm in comfort, this was the day for it, and tomorrow looks almost identical.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: The sweepstake has collapsed. My eldest says 'nearly' is winning on the ferry evidence and his friend says the ferry evidence is hearsay, a word he learned this week from a court programme. Two children have stopped speaking over it. I'm staying well out of it.

units.author: truthwatch_gil
units.text: So Bram confirms fuel went out and gear came back. Which is what I said: something is ending and something is starting. Nobody has explained which is which. I'll keep asking until somebody does.

units.author: morrow_unknown
units.text: The lights were on again tonight, the usual ones and the jetty one. Fewer moving about than last week, I think, though I might be counting wrong from this distance. I'm sorry, I keep posting the same thing. I suppose I just want someone to have written it down.

units.title: Can a crew of five clear 10,000 trees in 30 days? (Arithmetic only.)
units.author: skeptic_planner
units.text: Arithmetic only. The consent drawing estimates 'approximately 10,000 stems over 0.5 m girth'. Thirty days. If the crew is five fellers plus a lead, that is roughly 55 to 67 stems a head a day, depending on whether the lead cuts. Brash has to go somewhere, and the consent bars burning within 50 m of high water. I am not predicting anything. I am setting out the sum.

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: For comparison only: the 1890s camp's ledger records a best week of 312 stems for a gang of eleven men with axes and crosscut saws, so roughly four stems a man a day. The modern figure is about fifteen times that. Chainsaws are remarkable things. (Ledger B, folio 40.)

units.author: skeptic_ferrous
units.text: A useful post. I would add only that the per-tree payment rewards counting and the day rate rewards staying, so a site lead can be under pressure from both directions at once. None of that is mysterious. It is simply how such contracts are written.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: My eldest got this sum as homework, because his teacher used it as a 'real-life example', which I think is a bit much. He got 66.6 recurring and drew a tiny tree above the recurring dot. I'm counting that as a pass.

units.author: trades_holm_work
units.text: Thats about right. Add weather days: the storm week will have cost them two at least. Add the half-tide landing. Its a lot. On the other hand a good crew who dont stop for lunch can surprise you. I once did 90 in a day on spruce and couldnt lift a cup of tea for a week after.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Ninety in a day. Course you did. And I sold a hundred cars last Tuesday before my lunch.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Four a man a day with an axe, in midwinter, on an island. I keep thinking of the clerk adding them up by lamplight. Someone always has to do the counting. I hope whoever is counting now has a warmer hut and a better pen.

units.title: Rope Walk: collected. Credit where due.
units.author: sb_bins
units.text: Collected. 06:40, the green boxes on Rope Walk, all of them, including the two the gulls had opened, which the crew picked up by hand without complaint. I thanked them. They seemed surprised to be thanked. Credit where it is due. Bernard (Rope Walk)

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: Noted with pleasure, Bernard, and I'll pass your thanks to the waste team, who do not often receive any. I am marking this thread resolved, which is a word I have used rarely on this board this month.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Tollinby cardboard also collected, at last. The fort has been dismantled, with ceremony. My youngest gave a speech. It was mostly about the door. I've kept the sign.

units.title: Window lamps: a practical question from Tollinby.
units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: I asked last week whether to keep a lamp on like Gilliver folk do and was laughed at, kindly. I've thought about it and I'm going to. Not for any reason. The kids like it and the landing's dark. So, a practical question: what do people actually use? Candles feel like a fire risk with a cat and three children.

units.author: gilliver_lamp
units.text: My mother used an oil lamp with a glass chimney and I use a little electric one now, from the hardware shop, because of my hands. It doesnt matter what kind it is. It matters that it is on. Put it where it can be seen from outside, that is the whole of it. Its only manners.

units.author: sb_lostcat
units.text: I've had one on since Pebble came home, a little lamp with a paper shade in the front window. I'd not have said it was for anything. Reading this, I think it might be for the neighbours, so they can see I'm in and all right. Thank you for explaining it so simply.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Next you'll be leaving out a saucer of milk. It's an electricity bill with a story attached, that's all it is.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Electric it is, thank you. Bought one on the way home; the man in the hardware shop said I was the fourth from Tollinby this week, and that the Gilliver shop has sold out twice. The kids have named it. I'm not saying what.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: It is an electricity bill with a story attached, yes. Most of the good things in a house are. I keep a lamp in the shop window every night because I'm awake anyway, and once a man knocked at three to ask whether I sold maps. I did. He bought one and thanked me for being open.

units.title: Carrow Point station, 29th.
units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: 07:00: 1035 hPa, the highest reading this month. Air minus 2.6, grass minimum minus 5.1, wind calm. Sea smoke drifting off the creek below the lighthouse like a kettle left on. Visibility unlimited to seaward. The Met Office calls this 'settled'; I call it the best week for readings since the station went up.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Evening: 1034 hPa, starting to ease. Still calm. One thing I keep noticing in this cold spell: very little wind noise in the station's audio channel, so the night sounds come through very clean. Mostly the sea on the shingle. An owl twice. A dog in Gilliver, faintly, across the water.

units.title: Ferries & Roads: the Weyhaven night bus cuts.
units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: The Post reports three night routes going hourly. For the record, as a driver of thirty-one years: the 41 and 44 were half-empty after midnight since long before any power cuts, and the 47 has been run badly since they changed the depot. The 38 and the harbour circular are kept, which is correct. Light the shelters, they say. They said that in my day as well.

units.author: sb_roadworks
units.text: Same story on the Tollinby road: the late van run got cut back to one drop after the outages because nobody wanted to unload in the dark at the industrial estate. Still not back to two. Customers don't complain. They just come and collect in daylight now. Funny how fast that happened.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: Thank you, Wendell, for the routes, which I could not have supplied. The transport board's consultation on shelter lighting is open until the end of next month for anyone who would like to say so formally.

units.title: Found: reading glasses in a red case, Gilliver chippy.
units.author: gilliver_teen
units.text: found at the chippy tonight: reading glasses in a red case, left on the counter about 9. they're behind the till with the lost umbrellas. not trolling or anything, genuinely just glasses, and somebody can't read the menu without them

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Them's my brother's. He's been looking all over the house for them and blaming the dog. He'll be in on Friday for his haddock. Thank you, lad. That's decent of you.

units.title: Still not buying it (but the studio lights stay on)
units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: For the record, because people keep asking on air: I am still not buying the edge-of-the-light stuff. I've watched the story jump from a lighthouse to a car park to a bakery to my own phone lines in a fortnight, and every hop adds a detail. That said, I've stopped turning the studio lights down for the 3am music hour. Call it set dressing. Call it whatever you like.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: I rang in on the 21st, as some here know, and I've since said I may have misheard the name that caller gave. I'd hate to be one of your hops. Leave the lights up. The 3am hour sounds better with them on, though I couldn't tell you why.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Agreed with all of it. Lights up is fine. People perform worse in dim light at 3am whatever is or isn't outside; your producer's instinct is just good occupational health. I'll happily write you a note for management.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Big fan of the 3am hour on the run; we have it on in the porters' lodge. Someone rang in for 'something cheerful' last week and you played a sea shanty about a drowned man, which the lodge felt was a choice.

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: It was the only cheerful one in the box that night. Our music library has an unhealthy ratio of drowned men. I've put in a request for more songs where everybody gets home and has their tea.

units.author: morrow_unknown
units.text: I listen most nights. Sorry, I don't usually post here. I only wanted to say the studio lights don't come through on the radio, obviously, but somehow it sounds as if they're on. That's a silly thing to say. Thank you for doing the show.

units.title: Last night at the DC: I'm taking the day job
units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: Last shift tonight. Handing my scanner in at six and starting at the builders' merchant on Monday, eight till four, with a lunch break that has actual daylight in it. The yard lights still cut out about once a week for no reason and everyone still goes and stands in the dock doors when they do. I won't miss that. I'll miss the lads. And the satsuma economy.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Good luck, mate. Day work does strange things to your sense of time for about a fortnight; you'll be eating your dinner at eleven in the morning and then it settles. Control says congratulations, which is the first nice thing Control has said all year.

units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text: welcome to the daylight, I switched last week. people look different in the day, they talk more, they ask for the radio on, nobody falls asleep in the back. I'm not sure I like it yet. anyway good luck

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Congratulations. Sleep the whole first weekend, don't be a hero about switching. And take a satsuma in on your first day for whoever's on the next bench. Old ward tradition, invented just now. Back to it.

units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: Cheers, all. Control can come to the leaving drinks if he says it to my face. Last pick of the night was a box of nightlights, forty-eight to a pack, for a hardware shop in Gilliver. Third pallet of them this week. Make of that what you will, as the audio lot say.

units.title: Dog update: the back corridor, still
units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: Update on the back corridor, since people keep asking. The dogs still won't walk it after about two. Tonight it was Pepper, a young collie, who sat down at the fire door at 02:20 and leaned back on the lead like a mule. We've checked the vent again: no mouse, no smell, no draught. I walked her round the front instead. I'm not settling this. I've just changed the route.

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Dogs know their business. I had a heeler ride with me six years who wouldn't get out at one particular rest stop on the 40. Fine stop, good coffee, clean restrooms. She'd sit in the cab and that was that. I stopped using it. Cost me nothing but four miles.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Dogs are excellent sensors and terrible narrators. They're reacting to something real: a sound above our range, a smell, a pressure change when the ventilation cycles. Changing the route is the right call. You don't need to know why to respect a dog's no.

units.title: Patrol log, quiet week
units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Patrol log summary, week four. Patrols at 00:00, 02:00 and 04:00, nil found, every night. Camera 6 replaced again after salt damage. One container left open by the day shift, closed and reported. One fox, the same fox I think, now known to the day shift as the Inspector. Quietest week since I started.

units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: The Inspector comes to our back door too, I'm almost certain: same limp in the left hind leg. He gets the burnt ends of the baguettes. Our harbour has been very quiet as well, just gulls and the bread van. It's nice. I'd forgotten nice.

units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: Quiet weeks are the ones logbooks never mention, and they are most of the weeks. I read old keepers' logs for company sometimes, page after page of 'lamp checked, all well'. It is the most comforting reading I know, and I can't fully explain why.

units.title: The dead-air caller is back (it's an autodialler again)
units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: Remember the dead-air calls at the same minute each night that turned out to be an autodialler? They're back: 01:17, every night this week. IT says a different company has bought the same faulty system. So it's the same nothing, from someone new. I've named the number Gerald. Gerald never says anything. Gerald is my favourite caller.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: gerald is an icon. I'd like a gerald for my lab: someone who rings at the same time every night and expects nothing. instead I have a supervisor who emails at 01:17 asking about figure 4

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: Gerald is welcome here. Please don't post the number itself, in case someone decides to call Gerald back and it turns out to be a real person's line with a broken machine on it.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: update: emailed facilities like you said. they replaced the controller in week two, not the sensors. so: a plausible draught plus old sensors. chapter is 80% done. I'm choosing to believe in the draught because the draught doesn't need a methods section.

units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: Good choice. Draughts are reliable. I've worked with one for three years by the freezer aisle. Its name is Kenji. Kenji also doesn't need a methods section.

units.title: Streetlights back in town
units.author: lh_miner_vellmark
units.text: End of shift, on the bus. Council fixed the streetlights that went out last week. People still stand in their doorways at dusk, a minute or two, then go in. Not scared. Just looking. My mother does it. Says she's 'seeing the day off'.

units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: 'Seeing the day off.' I'm going to borrow that, with your mother's permission. It is what I do on the gallery every evening, and I've never had a phrase for it that didn't sound grander than it is.

units.title: From the cab tonight (not a thread starter, promise)
units.author: lh_crane_halvard
units.text: Back at the top. Not starting any big threads, don't worry. Just: the city from 60 m tonight is all frost and orange light, the ring road like a necklace. Someone down there is walking a dog in a reflective coat and I've watched them go round the park three times. Hope you're all warm.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: I think I can see your crane from the ward window: red light on the jib, by the river? If so, hello. The dog walker is very likely one of our night porters, who walks his terrier on his break and claims it is 'for the dog'.

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Glad to see you up there again. Your threads are welcome, the ordinary kind especially. Nobody here holds the other one against you; you closed it yourself, and kindly.

units.title: did anyone fix the roof door
units.author: dc_12_ollie
units.text: did anyone fix the roof door. my mum says i can ask one more thing on here and then i have to stop. it was unlocked again tuesday morning, i saw when i took the recycling up for Irena. is it supposed to be locked or not. nobody ever says

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Good question, Ollie, and thank you for taking Irena's recycling up. The roof door should be locked from the outside and openable from the inside with the push bar, in case of fire. I've reported it to Kerrow again with your date. Bev, DCRA

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: It's a door. Doors open. Some kid's going up there to vape. Mystery solved, you're welcome.

units.author: dc_9_tobin
units.text: Ollie's observation matches his earlier one: unlocked in the morning, nobody seen opening it. Explanations in order of likelihood: (1) contractor access to the aerial, (2) caretaker, (3) residents smoking on the roof. I've stopped counting footsteps. I haven't stopped making lists.

units.author: dc_14_ivy
units.text: (Hi Ollie.) It's supposed to be locked from outside; it's a fire door with a push bar, so it opens from the stairs but not from the roof. The chair I propped against it was moved. The caretaker probably moved it. Probably. I still haven't decided, and I've stopped propping things against doors.

units.title: Something nice (as Bev asked)
units.author: dc_5_lorna
units.text: Bev asked for something nice so here's mine love, the depot gave the night cleaners a tin of biscuits for getting through the outages with a note in it that said thank you for keeping the lights on, which we didn't, the power company did, but it was a lovely note and the biscuits were the good ones with chocolate on the bottom

units.author: dc_7_irena
units.text: Dear neighbours, a nice thing: my granddaughter has written from abroad to say she will visit at New Year and would like to learn the old embroidery stitches. I have found my husband's magnifying lamp for her. It works perfectly, which is more than I can say for the lift. Irena, 7C

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: Something nice. Fine. The 38 was on time twice this week and the driver said good morning to me both times. That is my nice thing. Do not expect another one.

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: This is exactly what I hoped for. Thank you, all of you. I'm printing these for the noticeboard by the lift, where people will have time to read them while it smells. Keep them coming. Bev, DCRA

units.author: dc_8_benedikt
units.text: Nice thing: my daughter's school sent home her drawing of our building and she drew all fourteen floors with a light in every window. It is on the fridge now. Sorry for spelling, I am typing in the van between drops.

units.author: dc_2_hassan
units.text: Nice thing from the shop: the bread man leaves a free loaf on Fridays for whoever is on their own. Irena has one, Wendell has one (he complains about it). If anyone else would like one, tell me. No need to say why. H

units.author: dc_6_jordie
units.text: nice thing: passed my thermodynamics resit. 61%. not glamorous but i'll take it. celebrated with chips and took the lift home like a king. still call the stairwell the cardio of doom. haven't done my cardio in a fortnight

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Credit to Garrick for checking. Structure-borne noise from a treadmill would be a steady train of thuds around 2.5 Hz at a fixed level; most reports describe steps moving between floors, which a fixed source doesn't do. My compressor idea is out too, now the chiller's known to be unplugged. I have nothing better to offer. One line, as usual: I was wrong.

units.author: dc_10_garrick
units.text: Respect, mate. If anyone wants to stand on the stairs at 05:00 and listen while I run, to rule me out properly, my door's open and the kettle's on. Offer stands. Nobody's taken it up yet, which tells you something.

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: Hassan, my car is in the loading bay because the disabled bay has a van in it. You can see how this goes. I will move my car to the street on Friday mornings if your bread man uses the loading bay. That is my final offer, and I want it minuted.

units.title: Back on the water (not the ferry)
units.author: deckhand_finn
units.text: Hi all, some of you asked. I'm on the Kittiwake now, creels out of Gilliver with Bram's cousin, mornings, home by two. Pay's worse, hours are better, nobody hails anything. I'm not talking about the other thing so please don't ask, I took it down for a reason. Just wanted to say I'm alright and she's a good boat.

units.author: ferry_mate_kerris
units.text: Good. Glad you're on the water. The deck's not the same without you singing badly on the ramp. Not asking you anything. Come for a drink when we're both off.

units.author: harbour_admin
units.text: Welcome back lad. The Kittiwake's account at the chandlery is in your cousin's name not yours so don't go signing for rope. Anyone asking Finn about the other thing gets a warning from me, no second one.

units.author: deckhand_finn
units.text: Cheers Kerris. I'll come for the drink. I'll even sing if you want, just not on the ramp, and not that one about the herring.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: He's a good hand. Ties a better knot than my cousin, which isn't saying much, but still. Leave him be about the rest of it, lads.

units.title: Floodlights on the night run: first week report
units.author: ferry_engineer_seth
units.text: First week with the new deck floods. Two 400 W LED heads on the wheelhouse roof and one on the ramp arm, fed off the house generator, which grumbles but copes. Fuel use up a hair. Berthing at Gilliver in last week's murk was easy. The slipway end is lit to the water now. Nothing to report on that front, and I'd like to keep it that way.

units.author: ferry_skipper_odell
units.text: Agreed. Passengers like them, crew like them. We crossed six nights this week without a single entry in the remarks column, which is how I prefer the remarks column. Logged it, carried on.

units.author: lisle_crew_ada
units.text: The Lisle slip is getting lights too... the ones on the pier office went up yesterday. I walked past at five on the way to the bakery and it was all lit right down to the water. It looks smaller lit. Ha. Most things do.

units.author: lineman_tess
units.text: If the house generator grumbles, check the load at switch-on: LED drivers can pull a spike when they all start together. Stagger them a second apart. Free advice from someone who's been reading about inrush current all week for her day-shift course.

units.title: Market prices this week
units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Prices at Port Ammet this week: lobster up a bit with the calm, brown crab steady, velvets not worth the diesel. A calm spell brings everyone out so the market fills up. Bait's gone up again. Lamp's lit, kettle's on, early start tomorrow.

units.author: harbour_admin
units.text: Bait's up because the supplier's van has been off the road. Should come back down next week he says. Velvets I can't help you with lads, nobody can, not even the restaurant in Port Ammet that used to take them.

units.author: harbourmaster_quill
units.text: Thank you to everyone who kept berth 3 clear this morning. The contractor's vessel loaded and sailed at 06:40 without delay. The same arrangement applies tomorrow, the 30th. I have not been told of any sailings after that, and I would ask members not to speculate about them in this thread.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: She'll be out again at half six. I'll be at the fuel berth before her. Holm jetty light still burning over the water, same as every night. If anyone wants to wave the boat off, the wall's free.

units.title: Reservoir dawn chorus, 29th (no knocks, sorry)
units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: First file since I got back. Brackwater reservoir, south dam, this morning 06:50 to 07:35. Two omnis on a 30 cm bar, gain at 42 dB, no dish. Robin, wren, a very confident blackbird, distant geese at 21:10 into the file, the overflow weir throughout. No percussive events. I went in daylight and came back in daylight. Make of it what you will.

units.author: tern_audio
units.text: ok so this is lovely. the blackbird at 4:30 is doing a thing where it copies a car alarm?? or a phone. I've put a spectrogram up with an arrow on it. welcome back to files. I missed your files. I'll stop now

units.author: hobby_binaural
units.text: Headphones on for this one. The geese pass from left to right behind the mics, beautifully placed, and the weir sits low and centred like a bed of noise under everything. A lovely, calm file. Thank you for sharing it.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: It's a phone, I think. There's a ringtone in town that every blackbird in Brackwater has learned. If you want, come up at the weekend and we'll do the north inlet together, in daylight, two rigs, synced clocks. Properly synced this time.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Thanks. A phone ringtone, I'd guess; the town blackbirds have all picked one up. I'm going to keep to daylight files for a while. Not for any particular reason. I just like the light at that end of the day.

units.author: tern_audio
units.text: yes. absolutely yes. I'll bring the good cables and sync the clocks twice and write the offset on my hand. thank you. (and sorry again about the clock thing in week two, I know I already said sorry)

units.author: lowband_mod
units.text: Moving this into the featured files list. This is what LowBand exists for: a raw file, a kit list, gain, times, and no story. Thank you, and welcome back to the archive queue.

units.author: nightscream_vlog
units.text: guys this is insane, I'm doing a reservoir livestream this weekend from the exact same spot, night time obviously, link in bio, gonna find out what everyone's so scared of up there

units.author: lowband_mod
units.text: nightscream, you're welcome to record at the reservoir if the estate allows it. The estate doesn't allow it after dark. Please don't promote streams in other people's threads. Next time it will be removed.

units.title: A question for the archive volunteers: print-through on old cassettes
units.author: hobby_tapeloop
units.text: Dear all, a question for whoever looks after the archive. Entry 2214, the 'BW gate, nights' cassette, lists two percussive events two minutes apart. Print-through would give a faint copy of a loud sound a second or two before or after it, from the next layer of tape, so two events that far apart are not print-through, I grant. But is there a pre-echo before each? That would tell us about the machine. Regards, Ned

units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: Ned, thank you, a fair question. The events are 2 min 04 s apart. I did find a faint pre-echo 1.6 s before each, which is print-through of the events themselves, and I've added that to the entry. The events remain unattributed. Your machinery view is noted in the curator's file, as always.

units.author: hobby_tapeloop
units.text: Thank you, most satisfying. A pre-echo of 1.6 seconds suggests a slow-speed portable, probably a cheap one left in the cold. Machinery, I still say: a gate chain, a keeper's vehicle, a pump house. And it is very good to see dunlin's name back on the board. Regards, Ned

units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: Checked for cycling. The hum runs continuously for all 52 minutes of the clip: no on, no off. So not a fridge on a thermostat, or else one that never reaches temperature. Nothing on the harbour fits that either. I'm putting this one down for a while. It's a pump. Somewhere.

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: A compressor that never cycles off is one that's struggling: warm surroundings, worn seals, or a door opened often. Could also be a cold-store condenser fan with a compressor-like tone. Sorry. I don't have a tidy answer for this one, and I'd rather say so.
